analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits for current and future retirees, taxing high earners' wages above the cap to help pay for it.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with the sponsor and 4 cosponsors, has sat in two House committees since June 2026 with no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would increase Social Security checks in three ways: a richer benefit formula for lower and middle earners, extra credit for earnings above the yearly wage cap, and a new cost-of-living index built around what retirees actually buy, especially medical care. It would also recompute benefits for people already retired, with a guarantee that nobody's check goes down. To help cover the cost, it would apply the payroll tax to wages above the annual cap starting in 2026 — though as written that tax phases down to nothing after four years, while the benefit increases are permanent.
analysis.who_benefits: Current Social Security beneficiaries and future retirees, especially lower- and middle-wage workers whose checks rise the most under the richer formula, plus people on disability and survivor benefits. Current retirees would get their benefits recomputed upward, and the switch to an elderly-consumer price index would raise future annual increases because seniors' spending — particularly on medical care — tends to rise faster than the general index.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: Raises the replacement rate for the lowest bracket of career earnings from 90 percent to 95 percent, which lifts benefits most for the lowest-paid workers.

Adds a higher second step to the benefit formula starting in 2026 and growing over time, reaching 15 percent above today's formula for people retiring after 2045, which raises benefits for middle earners.
For the first time counts wages above the annual Social Security cap in benefit calculations at a reduced 5 percent rate, so high earners who pay more also draw somewhat more.

Directs the Social Security Administration to recompute benefits for everyone already on the rolls under the improved formula, and guarantees no beneficiary's check can be lowered by the recomputation.

Replaces the cost-of-living formula's price index with a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers that the Bureau of Labor Statistics would build, tracking the spending of people at retirement age, where medical costs weigh more heavily.

analysis.who_pays: High earners whose wages exceed the annual Social Security tax cap (about $176,000 in 2025) would owe payroll tax on a share of wages above it — 80 percent in 2026, declining 20 points a year until the above-cap tax reaches zero in 2030. Self-employed high earners face the same. Employers also face new withholding duties on above-cap wages during those years, and taxpayers fund the new price index.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners above the payroll tax cap

drawbacks.text: The financing is temporary while the benefits are permanent: the tax on wages above the cap falls to zero by 2030, but the higher benefit formula, the extra bend point growing to 15 percent, and the CPI-E cost-of-living increases run indefinitely — so as written, the bill adds far more in lifetime benefit obligations than the four years of extra revenue it collects, and would likely deepen the program's projected shortfall rather than fix it.
High earners and self-employed professionals would face a new payroll tax on earnings above roughly $176,000 for 2026 through 2029, a real cost concentrated on the top few percent of earners.

The CPI-E index the bill mandates would almost certainly produce larger annual increases than the current index, because retirees' spending — medical care in particular — rises faster than the overall price index, adding to the program's long-term cost on top of the richer benefit formula.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit increases are real and reach tens of millions of current and future retirees, with the largest gains going to lower and middle earners — and the no-cut guarantee protects people already retired. But the bill is not honestly paid for as drafted: it taxes above-cap wages for only four years while making every benefit expansion permanent, so its title's promise to make Social Security stronger for future generations does not match its text. A version that kept the above-cap tax in place permanently would be far more fiscally coherent.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2026 and split between two House committees, and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Lateefah Simon introduced the bill on June 23, 2026.

The Speaker referred it to the Ways and Means Committee and, additionally, to the Education and Workforce Committee, the standard route that leaves the first committee in control of whether it ever moves.
Four House Democrats have cosponsored it; no further action of any kind appears in the record since the referral.
Republicans hold 223 of the House's 441 seats, so a bill raising payroll taxes on high earners to fund benefit increases would need support well beyond its sponsor's party to reach the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, high earners above the payroll cap keep all of that income untaxed and Social Security benefits remain as they are — the bill has gained nothing and lost nothing yet, sitting in committees run by the majority party, which has taken no action on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners above the cap; beneficiaries unchanged

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee majority
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee of primary referral has taken no action on the bill — no hearing or markup has been scheduled since it arrived in June 2026.

against.name: Speaker of the House
against.what_they_did: Split the bill between two committees on referral, leaving Ways and Means in control; no floor action has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: Every supporter in the record is a Democrat — the sponsor plus 4 of 217 House Democrats — and no Republican has cosponsored; no member has yet voted or spoken against it, but with Republicans holding 223 of 441 House seats, a payroll-tax increase on high earners has no evident path to the floor.

industries.industry: High-income households (wages above the Social Security cap)
industries.note: The bill would tax 80 percent of wages above the roughly $176,000 cap in 2026, phasing down to zero by 2030 — a new cost for the top few percent of earners. Keeping that income untaxed is the benefit they would lose, and it is exactly what funds the benefit increases for ordinary retirees, so their interest in the bill runs directly against beneficiaries'.
The bill applies the same above-cap tax to self-employment income for 2026 through 2029, hitting high-earning independent contractors, partners, and small business owners on income above the cap.

Employers would need to withhold and report payroll tax on wages above the cap during the four-year phase-in, adding compliance work, though the burden is administrative rather than a direct tax since the employer share above the cap is not imposed.

analysis.trajectory: The Congress is still in session, but this bill's path is the one most private members' bills take: with four cosponsors, no Republican support, and committees under a 223-seat Republican majority that has taken no action, it is very likely to sit in committee until the session ends in January 2027 without a vote. A Democratic Social Security expansion of this kind would need either a House majority change or a much broader bipartisan coalition, neither of which is visible in the record.
